text: InsectSprays counts insects plots treated six sprays. checks show box plot : two groups right-skewed, spreads differ threefold, response counts. ANOVA data unreliable. log transformation textbook fix, counts zeros need log(y + 1), biases estimates (O’Hara Kotze 2010); count GLM models variance growing mean directly, tidyvisor recommends negative binomial GLM. rank test (Kruskal-Wallis) robust test listed alternatives.

A count GLM models #> that directly and gives each group difference as a ratio of means; transforming #> counts (log(y + 1)) biases the estimates (O'Hara and Kotze 2010). The variance #> is up to 2.3 times the mean, so the negative binomial. #> m <- MASS::glm.nb(count ~ spray, data = data) #> anova(m, test = "Chisq"); tidyvisor(m) #> Alternative: Non-parametric: rank test #> Makes no assumption about the shape of the distributions; answers whether #> values in one group tend to be larger. #> kruskal.test(count ~ spray, data = data) #> pairwise.wilcox.test(data$count, data$spray, p.adjust.method = "holm") #> Alternative: Robust: trimmed means #> Resists outliers and heavy tails while still comparing a centre. #> WRS2::t1way(count ~ spray, data = data)   # 20% trimmed means #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the result #> What was tested, the effect with its interval, and what to do next. #> tidyvisor(result)

what: After the test: what does it say, and what next?
title: 3. Checking assumptions and choosing the test
text: classical test result can explained:
code: tidyvisor(kruskal.test(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays)) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test on count by spray. #>  #> ── Result ── #>  #> • Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 54.7 (df = 5), p < 0.001. #>  #> ── Meaning ── #>  #> • Values in one group tend to be larger than in another. Rank tests compare #>   whole distributions, not means: report medians or the location shift with its #>   interval, not a difference in means. #> • A p-value is not the size of an effect: always report the estimate and its #>   interval, and a non-significant result is not evidence of no difference. #>  #> ── After the overall test ── #>  #> • The overall test shows that the 6 groups are not all alike; it does not say #>   which differ. Go on to post hoc comparisons of every pair, with p-values #>   adjusted for the number of comparisons. #> • Rank-based pairs (the follow-up to Kruskal-Wallis): #>   pairwise.wilcox.test(data$count, data$spray, p.adjust.method = "holm"), or a #>   Dunn test (FSA::dunnTest(count ~ spray, data = data, method = "holm")). #> • Report each pair as a median difference or Hodges-Lehmann shift with its #>   interval (wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE)), not only adjusted p-values. #> • Decide which pairs matter before looking: if only comparisons with a control #>   are of interest, test those alone (Dunnett, or Holm on that smaller set); #>   fewer comparisons keep more power. #>  #> ── What to do next ── #>  #> • For an effect size, wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE) gives the Hodges-Lehmann #>   shift with its interval. #> • If the data are positive and right-skewed, a test on the log scale (or a #>   Gamma GLM) gives a ratio of means, which is often easier to report. #>  #> ── For the paper ── #>  #> • Results: 'count differed among levels of spray (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test; #>   H(5) = 54.7, p < 0.001).' #> • Report the statistic with its degrees of freedom, the exact p-value (p < #>   0.001 below that), and the effect size with its interval; never 'p = 0.000' #>   or 'n.s.' alone. #> • Figure: #> • ggplot2::ggplot(data, ggplot2::aes(spray, count)) + #>   ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) + #>   ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) + #>   ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 9) #> • ggplot2::ggsave("figure1.pdf", width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm") # one #>   journal column #> • Figure style for journals: show the raw data with the estimates, give n per #>   group in the caption, label axes with units, use a colour-blind-safe palette #>   (Okabe-Ito, viridis) and no 3D, pie or dual-axis charts; text at least 8 pt #>   at final size; save as PDF or SVG (vector) at the journal's column width #>   (about 85 mm single, 180 mm double), or 600 dpi for raster images. #> • Table: one row per level of spray with n and the median and interquartile #>   range; the test in a footnote, and any post hoc results as letters or a #>   pairwise table with adjusted p-values. #> • Methods: name the test (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test), the software and #>   version (R 4.6.2, citation()), any adjustment for multiple comparisons, and #>   the significance level. tidyvisor(shapiro.test(InsectSprays$count)) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Shapiro-Wilk normality test on InsectSprays$count. #>  #> ── Result ── #>  #> • W = 0.922, p < 0.001. #>  #> ── Meaning ── #>  #> • The data depart from normality. With large samples this flags even small #>   departures; look at the Q-Q plot before acting. #> • A p-value is not the size of an effect: always report the estimate and its #>   interval, and a non-significant result is not evidence of no difference. #>  #> ── What to do next ── #>  #> • Positive, right-skewed data: try a log transformation (or find the best power #>   with MASS::boxcox()), then test again on the new scale. #> • Outliers or heavy tails: use a robust method (trimmed means with WRS2::yuen() #>   or WRS2::t1way(); MASS::rlm() for regression). #> • Otherwise, or with small groups: a rank test (wilcox.test(), kruskal.test()) #>   or a permutation test. #> • With 30 or more values per group, tests on means are usually still valid #>   (central limit theorem); check the conclusion with a rank test. #>  #> ── For the paper ── #>  #> • Assumption checks are not results: state in the Methods which checks were #>   made and what was done about them (for example 'Normality of residuals was #>   checked with Q-Q plots; counts were log-transformed'). #> • A formal test of an assumption is rarely worth reporting on its own; the plot #>   of the residuals is more informative.

what: After a model: what to do when the residuals fail
title: 3. Checking assumptions and choosing the test
text: linear model, interpretation ends next, chosen checks failed. model insect counts: positive, right-skewed response whose spread grows mean, log scale Gamma GLM remedy:
code: m <- lm(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays) tidyvisor(m)$sections[["What to do next"]] #> [1] "count is counts: fit a Poisson or negative binomial GLM instead of a linear model (glm(..., family = poisson) or MASS::glm.nb()); it models the variance growing with the mean. Avoid log(y + 1), which biases the estimates (O'Hara and Kotze 2010)." #> [2] "After any change, check the residuals again with plot() and tidyvisor()." set.seed(2) d <- data.frame(x = runif(80, 1, 10)) d$y <- exp(0.3 * d$x + rnorm(80, 0, 0.6)) tidyvisor(lm(y ~ x, data = d))$sections[["What to do next"]] #> [1] "Transform the response: the values are positive and the residuals are right-skewed with a spread that grows with the fitted values, which a log scale often fixes. Refit with log(y) and check again; effects then multiply y (report exp(coefficient)). MASS::boxcox(m) shows which power suits the data (0 = log, 0.5 = square root)." #> [2] "Or keep the original scale with a Gamma GLM and a log link, which expects the spread to grow with the mean: glm(y ~ x, family = Gamma(link = \"log\"), data = data)."                                                                                                                                                                    #> [3] "Keep the model but make the standard errors robust to unequal variance: lmtest::coeftest(m, vcov = sandwich::vcovHC(m, type = \"HC3\")). Or model the variance with weights (nlme::gls(..., weights = varPower()))."                                                                                                                     #> [4] "Rank-based or permutation alternatives make no assumption about the distribution: for one factor, kruskal.test() or wilcox.test(); for a whole model, a permutation test of each term (for example lmPerm::lmp())."                                                                                                                      #> [5] "After any change, check the residuals again with plot() and tidyvisor()."

title: 7. Community and spatial ecology
text: dune meadow data pair species cover 20 plots soil management plot. Give species site variables; tidyvisor measures gradient length follows CANOCO rule: 3 standard deviations linear method (PCA, RDA), 4 unimodal one (CA, CCA), either . result analysis can explained turn:
code: data(dune, dune.env, package = "vegan") d <- cbind(dune, dune.env) tidyvisor(d, question = "vegan", species = names(dune),           env = c("A1", "Management")) #> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'parsnip': #>   method          from  #>   print.nullmodel vegan #>  #> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: vegan #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Sites: 20 #> • Species: 30 #> • Zeros: 67% — many zeros: avoid Euclidean distances on raw counts (double-zero #>   problem); use Hellinger or Bray-Curtis #> • Gradient length (longest DCA axis, SD units): 3.52 — between 3 and 4 SD: #>   intermediate; linear and unimodal methods are both appropriate #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Model: Redundancy analysis (RDA) on Hellinger-transformed abundances #> Branch: constrained ordination (a picture of the gradients your variables #> explain, tested by permutation). With a gradient of 3 to 4 SD, linear and #> unimodal methods are both appropriate; CCA (vegan::cca(comm ~ ...)) is the #> alternative. The Hellinger transformation removes the double-zero problem so #> RDA can be used on community data (Legendre & Gallagher 2001). #> comm <- data[species] #> m <- vegan::rda(vegan::decostand(comm, "hellinger") ~ A1 + Management, data = data) #> Test: Permutation tests of the model, the axes and each term #> Community data are not multivariate normal; permutations give valid p-values. #> anova(m); anova(m, by = "terms"); vegan::RsquareAdj(m) #> Alternative: PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities #> Branch: multivariate test (a p-value, no picture). Tests differences in #> composition without assuming a linear or unimodal response (Anderson 2001). #> vegan::adonis2(comm ~ A1 + Management, data = data, method = "bray", by = "terms") #> Check: Compare the dispersion of the Management groups #> PERMANOVA is sensitive to differences in spread as well as location; a #> significant betadisper test means a PERMANOVA difference may reflect spread. #> b <- vegan::betadisper(vegan::vegdist(comm), data$Management); anova(b) #> Groups: To find the species combinations that best separate the Management #> groups: canonical variate analysis #> CVA (discriminant analysis) maximises the separation between predefined groups; #> it needs fewer species than sites, so use a few species or the first PCA axes. #> tidydiversity::ord_cva(data, abundance = abundance, group = "Management") #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the result #> Variance explained, tests and how to read the plot. #> tidyvisor(m) r <- vegan::rda(vegan::decostand(dune, "hellinger") ~ A1 + Management,                 data = dune.env) tidyvisor(r) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Redundancy analysis (RDA) of 20 sites with 4 constraining degrees of freedom. #>  #> ── Fit ── #>  #> • The explanatory variables account for 38.6% of the total variance (adjusted #>   R-squared 22.2%, corrected for the number of variables). #> • The first constrained axis shows 17.5% of the total. #>  #> ── Tests ── #>  #> • Whole model: F = 2.35, p = 0.002 (999 permutations). #> • A1 explains 13.0% of the variation: F = 3.17, p = 0.004. #> • Management explains 25.6% of the variation: F = 2.08, p = 0.008. #>  #> ── Reading the plot ── #>  #> • In an RDA triplot, the angle between arrows approximates correlation; project #>   sites or species onto an arrow to read their relation to it. #> • Look at the axes' explained variance before reading patterns along them.

You want to describe the main patterns #> of composition, not test their causes. #> Method: CA, or NMDS #> Gradient length 11.6 SD; NMDS on bray dissimilarity suits any data. #> ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "ca", transform = "none") #> ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "nmds", distance = "bray") #> Interpret: Fit site variables afterwards (arrows, contours, centroids) #> Fitted variables are a post hoc interpretation of the axes; their permutation #> p-values are descriptive. #> autoplot(ord, surface = <numeric variable>) #> Check: Scree diagram (PCA, CA) or Shepard diagram and stress (NMDS) #> How many axes are worth reading, and how faithful the diagram is. #> autoplot(ord, type = "scree")   # or type = "shepard" #> Plots: Biplot with numeric variables as contours or symbol size, factors as #> centroids; scree or Shepard inset; stability ellipses #> Contours show non-linear change that an arrow hides; the inset shows how #> faithful the diagram is; ellipses show which sites are placed firmly. #> autoplot(ord, surface = <numeric>, colour = <factor>, inset = "scree")   # "shepard" for NMDS #> autoplot(ord, type = "gradient", path = <numeric>) #> autoplot(ord, type = "stability") #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the tables and the diagram #> Variation explained, tests, directions of variables, groups, species at each #> end of the axes, and how to read the plot. #> ord_interpret(ord)

code: tidyvisor(InsectSprays, response = "count", group = "spray") #> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'parsnip': #>   method          from  #>   print.nullmodel vegan #>  #> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: compare #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Groups: 6 — A (n = 12), B (n = 12), C (n = 12), D (n = 12), E (n = 12), F (n #>   = 12) #> • Normality (Shapiro-Wilk p, per group): A 0.75; B 0.64; C 0.048; D 0.0027; E #>   0.3; F 0.1 — at least one group departs from normality #> • Skewness: A 0.27; B -0.35; C 1.13; D 1.68; E 0.05; F 0.39 — right-skewed #>   (long tail of large values) #> • Outliers (robust z > 3.5): 0 #> • Spread (largest SD / smallest SD): 3.59 (Fligner-Killeen p = 0.013) — unequal #>   spreads: Student's t and the classical ANOVA are unreliable, especially with #>   unequal group sizes #> • Counts: non-negative whole numbers — counts have a variance that grows with #>   the mean; a GLM for counts models that directly #> • All values positive: no #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Before testing: Plot the data #> Box plots with the points show skewness, outliers and unequal spread at a #> glance; the checks above put numbers on them. #> boxplot(count ~ spray, data = data); stripchart(count ~ spray, data = data, vertical = TRUE, add = TRUE, method = "jitter") #> Test: GLM for counts: negative binomial #> The response is counts whose spread differs between groups. A count GLM models #> that directly and gives each group difference as a ratio of means; transforming #> counts (log(y + 1)) biases the estimates (O'Hara and Kotze 2010). The variance #> is up to 2.3 times the mean, so the negative binomial. #> m <- MASS::glm.nb(count ~ spray, data = data) #> anova(m, test = "Chisq"); tidyvisor(m) #> Alternative: Non-parametric: rank test #> Makes no assumption about the shape of the distributions; answers whether #> values in one group tend to be larger. #> kruskal.test(count ~ spray, data = data) #> pairwise.wilcox.test(data$count, data$spray, p.adjust.method = "holm") #> Alternative: Robust: trimmed means #> Resists outliers and heavy tails while still comparing a centre. #> WRS2::t1way(count ~ spray, data = data)   # 20% trimmed means #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the result #> What was tested, the effect with its interval, and what to do next. #> tidyvisor(result)

code: nb <- MASS::glm.nb(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays) tidyvisor(nb) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Generalised linear model of count on 72 observations (Negative #>   Binomial(28.0995) family, log link). #>  #> ── Fit ── #>  #> • The predictors explain 76.3% of the deviance (the GLM analogue of R-squared). #> • Against a model with no predictors: F = 42.06 on 5 and 66 df, p < 0.001. #>  #> ── Effects ── #>  #> • sprayB: spray = B (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   1.06 (+6%; 95% CI 0.814 to 1.37), p = 0.669. #> • sprayC: spray = C (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   0.144 (-86%; 95% CI 0.0913 to 0.226), p < 0.001. #> • sprayD: spray = D (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   0.339 (-66%; 95% CI 0.242 to 0.475), p < 0.001. #> • sprayE: spray = E (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   0.241 (-76%; 95% CI 0.166 to 0.352), p < 0.001. #> • sprayF: spray = F (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   1.15 (+15%; 95% CI 0.888 to 1.49), p = 0.281. #> • Effects on the log or logit scale are multiplicative: they combine by #>   multiplying, and a factor of 1 means no effect. #> • Each effect is estimated with the other predictors held fixed. #>  #> ── Diagnostics ── #>  #> • Influence: no observation dominates the fit (largest Cook's distance 0.18, #>   row 27; values above 1 would be a concern). #>  #> ── After the overall test ── #>  #> • spray (6 levels) has an overall effect (p < 0.001): the levels are not all #>   alike. Go on to post hoc comparisons of every pair, adjusted for the number #>   of comparisons; the coefficients above only compare each level with the #>   reference level A. #> • emmeans::emmeans(m, pairwise ~ spray, type = "response") # Tukey-adjusted #>   pairs, with intervals #> • If only comparisons with a control matter, decide so before looking and use #>   emmeans::emmeans(m, trt.vs.ctrl ~ spray, type = "response") (Dunnett; the #>   first level, A, is the control), which keeps more power. #>  #> ── For the paper ── #>  #> • Results (strongest evidence first; each factor level is compared with the #>   reference level): #> • 'count was 0.144 times as high for spray = C as for spray = A (95% CI 0.0913 #>   to 0.226, p < 0.001).' #> • 'count was 0.241 times as high for spray = E as for spray = A (95% CI 0.166 #>   to 0.352, p < 0.001).' #> • 'count was 0.339 times as high for spray = D as for spray = A (95% CI 0.242 #>   to 0.475, p < 0.001).' #> • The model is on the log scale, so effects are reported as ratios of means #>   (exponentiated coefficients) with their intervals. #> • Report every term of the model, not only the significant ones, with the #>   estimate, its 95% CI and the p-value; give n, and the fit (R-squared, or #>   deviance explained, or the random-effect SDs for a mixed model). #> • Figure: model predictions with their confidence band over the raw data, one #>   panel per focal predictor: #> • ggeffects::ggpredict(m, terms = "spray") |> plot(show_data = TRUE) #> • ggplot2::ggsave("figure1.pdf", width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm") # one #>   journal column #> • Figure style for journals: show the raw data with the estimates, give n per #>   group in the caption, label axes with units, use a colour-blind-safe palette #>   (Okabe-Ito, viridis) and no 3D, pie or dual-axis charts; text at least 8 pt #>   at final size; save as PDF or SVG (vector) at the journal's column width #>   (about 85 mm single, 180 mm double), or 600 dpi for raster images. #> • Table: one row per term with the estimate, 95% CI and p-value (and the #>   random-effect SDs for a mixed model): #> • gtsummary::tbl_regression(m, exponentiate = TRUE) # or broom::tidy(m, #>   conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) for your own table #> • Methods: the model formula, the family and link, how the model was checked, #>   the software and packages with versions (R 4.6.2; what: 5. A check with a rank test
title: Comparing treatments with counts
text: analyses agree sprays differ; count model also says much.
code: tidyvisor(kruskal.test(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays)) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test on count by spray. #>  #> ── Result ── #>  #> • Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 54.7 (df = 5), p < 0.001. #>  #> ── Meaning ── #>  #> • Values in one group tend to be larger than in another. Rank tests compare #>   whole distributions, not means: report medians or the location shift with its #>   interval, not a difference in means. #> • A p-value is not the size of an effect: always report the estimate and its #>   interval, and a non-significant result is not evidence of no difference. #>  #> ── After the overall test ── #>  #> • The overall test shows that the 6 groups are not all alike; it does not say #>   which differ. Go on to post hoc comparisons of every pair, with p-values #>   adjusted for the number of comparisons. #> • Rank-based pairs (the follow-up to Kruskal-Wallis): #>   pairwise.wilcox.test(data$count, data$spray, p.adjust.method = "holm"), or a #>   Dunn test (FSA::dunnTest(count ~ spray, data = data, method = "holm")). #> • Report each pair as a median difference or Hodges-Lehmann shift with its #>   interval (wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE)), not only adjusted p-values. #> • Decide which pairs matter before looking: if only comparisons with a control #>   are of interest, test those alone (Dunnett, or Holm on that smaller set); #>   fewer comparisons keep more power. #>  #> ── What to do next ── #>  #> • For an effect size, wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE) gives the Hodges-Lehmann #>   shift with its interval. #> • If the data are positive and right-skewed, a test on the log scale (or a #>   Gamma GLM) gives a ratio of means, which is often easier to report. #>  #> ── For the paper ── #>  #> • Results: 'count differed among levels of spray (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test; #>   H(5) = 54.7, p < 0.001).' #> • Report the statistic with its degrees of freedom, the exact p-value (p < #>   0.001 below that), and the effect size with its interval; never 'p = 0.000' #>   or 'n.s.' alone. #> • Figure: #> • ggplot2::ggplot(data, ggplot2::aes(spray, count)) + #>   ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) + #>   ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) + #>   ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 9) #> • ggplot2::ggsave("figure1.pdf", width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm") # one #>   journal column #> • Figure style for journals: show the raw data with the estimates, give n per #>   group in the caption, label axes with units, use a colour-blind-safe palette #>   (Okabe-Ito, viridis) and no 3D, pie or dual-axis charts; text at least 8 pt #>   at final size; save as PDF or SVG (vector) at the journal's column width #>   (about 85 mm single, 180 mm double), or 600 dpi for raster images. #> • Table: one row per level of spray with n and the median and interquartile #>   range; the test in a footnote, and any post hoc results as letters or a #>   pairwise table with adjusted p-values. #> • Methods: name the test (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test), the software and #>   version (R 4.6.2, citation()), any adjustment for multiple comparisons, and #>   the significance level.

code: tidyvisor(ChickWeight, question = "design", response = "weight",           group = "Diet", unit = "Chick", time = "Time") #> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'parsnip': #>   method          from  #>   print.nullmodel vegan #>  #> ── tidyvisor: is the design sound? ───────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: design #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Rows and columns: 578 rows, 4 columns #> • Missing values: none #> • Duplicated rows: 0 #> • Response: whole numbers, large: probably a measurement rounded to whole units #>   — If these are counts, use a Poisson or negative binomial model; if a #>   measurement, a linear model (or Gamma for positive skewed values). #> • Groups: 4 — 1 (220), 2 (120), 3 (120), 4 (118) #> • Units: 50 units, 11.6 rows per unit — several measurements per unit: they are #>   not independent #> • Unit of replication: Chick (treatment applied to whole units) — true #>   replicates (Chicks) per group: Diet 1: 20, Diet 2: 10, Diet 3: 10, Diet 4: #>   10; not the number of rows #> • Time points: 12 — repeated over time: residuals may be autocorrelated #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Design: Treat Chick as the unit of replication #> Each Chick received one treatment, so its 11.6 measurements are #> pseudoreplicates (Hurlbert 1984). Analyse with a random effect for Chick, or #> average within each Chick; counting rows as replicates makes p-values far too #> small. #> Design: Allow for correlation over time #> Measurements close in time are more alike; check the autocorrelation of the #> residuals and, if needed, add a temporal correlation structure (nlme::corAR1(), #> glmmTMB::ar1()). #> acf(residuals(m)) #> Analysis: Mixed model #> Chosen from the kind of response and the structure of the design; ask tidyvisor #> for the detailed advice and the assumption checks. #> lme4::lmer(weight ~ Diet + Time + (1 | Chick), data = data) #> # detailed advice: tidyvisor(data, response = "weight", random = "Chick") #> Next: Good practice for the rest of the study #> Pre-registration, data management, effect sizes and reporting guidelines. #> tv_practice()

text: mixed model random intercept slope chick lets grow rate, tests whether diets change average rate (diet--time interaction).
code: tidyvisor(ChickWeight, response = "weight", predictors = c("Time", "Diet"),           random = "Chick") #>  #> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: mixed #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Observations: 578 #> • Response: counts (non-negative integers) #> • Variance / mean: 41.5 — above 1: overdispersed; a negative binomial model is #>   safer than Poisson #> • Zeros: 0% observed, 0% expected under Poisson #> • Parameters (excluding intercept): 4 #> • Levels of Chick: 50 (observations per level: 2 to 12, median 12) #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Model: Generalised linear mixed model (lme4) #> Observations in the same group are not independent; random intercepts for Chick #> account for it and let the results generalise to other groups (Bolker et al. #> 2009). The counts are overdispersed, so the negative binomial is used. #> m <- lme4::glmer.nb(weight ~ Time + Diet + (1 | Chick), data = data) #> Random slopes: Consider a random slope for a predictor that varies within #> groups #> If the effect of a predictor differs among groups, a random intercept alone #> makes its p-value too small. #> (1 + Time | Chick) #> Before fitting: Plot the response against each predictor #> Shows non-linear relations, outliers and interactions that the model would miss #> (Zuur et al. 2010). #> plot(data[c("weight", "Time", "Diet")]) #> After fitting: Check the residuals #> Residual plots show non-linearity, unequal variance and influential points; #> tidyvisor reports the tests. #> plot(m)   # or performance::check_model(m) #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the model #> Fixed effects on the scale of the response, random-effect variances and #> diagnostics. #> tidyvisor(m) m <- lme4::lmer(weight ~ Time * Diet + (Time | Chick), data = ChickWeight) tidyvisor(m) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Linear mixed model of weight on 578 observations in 50 levels of Chick #>   (gaussian family, identity link), fitted with lme4. #>  #> ── Random effects ── #>  #> • Chick: (Intercept) varies with a standard deviation of 10.8 (in units of #>   weight). #> • Chick: Time varies with a standard deviation of 3.30 (in units of weight). #> • Residual standard deviation 12.8. Intra-class correlation 0.42: 42% of the #>   variance left after the fixed effects lies between groups. #>  #> ── Effects ── #>  #> • Time: each one-unit increase in Time changes weight by 6.28 (95% CI 4.78 to #>   7.77), p < 0.001. #> • Diet2: Diet = 2 (compared with Diet = 1) changes weight by -5.03 (95% CI #>   -14.8 to 4.79), p = 0.316. #> • Diet3: Diet = 3 (compared with Diet = 1) changes weight by -15.4 (95% CI #>   -25.2 to -5.59), p = 0.002. #> • Diet4: Diet = 4 (compared with Diet = 1) changes weight by -1.75 (95% CI #>   -11.6 to 8.08), p = 0.727. #> • Time:Diet2: each one-unit increase in Time:Diet2 changes weight by 2.33 (95% #>   CI -0.224 to 4.89), p = 0.074. #> • Time:Diet3: each one-unit increase in Time:Diet3 changes weight by 5.15 (95% #>   CI 2.59 to 7.70), p < 0.001. #> • Time:Diet4: each one-unit increase in Time:Diet4 changes weight by 3.25 (95% #>   CI 0.697 to 5.81), p = 0.013. #> • lmer() gives no p-values; those shown use the normal approximation (Wald z), #>   which is optimistic with few groups. For small samples, use lmerTest or a #>   parametric bootstrap. #> • Fixed effects are for a typical group (random effects at zero), with the #>   other predictors held fixed. #>  #> ── Diagnostics ── #>  #> • Normality of residuals (Shapiro-Wilk): W = 0.987, p < 0.001; code: library(tidyvisor) tv_practice("plan", design = "experiment") #>  #> ── tidyvisor: good research practice ─────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: practice #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Stage: plan #> • Study: experiment #> • Field: general #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Plan: Write the question and the hypothesis before collecting data #> A precise question decides the design, the response, the unit of replication #> and the analysis; analyses chosen after seeing the data inflate false #> positives. #> Plan: Define the unit of replication #> The unit to which a treatment is applied independently (plot, site, cage, #> patient, school) sets the sample size. Measurements within a unit are not #> replicates (pseudoreplication; Hurlbert 1984). #> Plan: Run a power analysis #> Decide the sample size from the smallest effect worth detecting, not from habit #> or budget alone. #> tv_power("two_groups", delta = <difference to detect>, sd = <standard deviation>) #> Plan: Randomise, include controls and blind where possible #> Randomising which unit gets which treatment removes systematic bias; controls #> give the baseline; blinding observers prevents expectations from colouring #> measurements. #> Plan: Pre-register the study and the analysis plan #> Recording hypotheses, design and analysis before the data exist separates #> confirmatory from exploratory results (Nosek et al. 2018). tidyvisor(ChickWeight, question = "design", response = "weight",           group = "Diet", unit = "Chick", time = "Time") #>  #> ── tidyvisor: is the design sound? ───────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: design #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Rows and columns: 578 rows, 4 columns #> • Missing values: none #> • Duplicated rows: 0 #> • Response: whole numbers, large: probably a measurement rounded to whole units #>   — If these are counts, use a Poisson or negative binomial model; if a #>   measurement, a linear model (or Gamma for positive skewed values). #> • Groups: 4 — 1 (220), 2 (120), 3 (120), 4 (118) #> • Units: 50 units, 11.6 rows per unit — several measurements per unit: they are #>   not independent #> • Unit of replication: Chick (treatment applied to whole units) — true #>   replicates (Chicks) per group: Diet 1: 20, Diet 2: 10, Diet 3: 10, Diet 4: #>   10; not the number of rows #> • Time points: 12 — repeated over time: residuals may be autocorrelated #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Design: Treat Chick as the unit of replication #> Each Chick received one treatment, so its 11.6 measurements are #> pseudoreplicates (Hurlbert 1984). Analyse with a random effect for Chick, or #> average within each Chick; counting rows as replicates makes p-values far too #> small. #> Design: Allow for correlation over time #> Measurements close in time are more alike; check the autocorrelation of the #> residuals and, if needed, add a temporal correlation structure (nlme::corAR1(), #> glmmTMB::ar1()). #> acf(residuals(m)) #> Analysis: Mixed model #> Chosen from the kind of response and the structure of the design; ask tidyvisor #> for the detailed advice and the assumption checks. #> lme4::lmer(weight ~ Diet + Time + (1 | Chick), data = data) #> # detailed advice: tidyvisor(data, response = "weight", random = "Chick") #> Next: Good practice for the rest of the study #> Pre-registration, data management, effect sizes and reporting guidelines. #> tv_practice()

You want to describe the main patterns #> of composition, not test their causes. #> Method: CA, or NMDS #> Gradient length 11.6 SD; NMDS on bray dissimilarity suits any data. #> ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "ca", transform = "none") #> ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "nmds", distance = "bray") #> Interpret: Fit site variables afterwards (arrows, contours, centroids) #> Fitted variables are a post hoc interpretation of the axes; their permutation #> p-values are descriptive. #> autoplot(ord, surface = <numeric variable>) #> Check: Scree diagram (PCA, CA) or Shepard diagram and stress (NMDS) #> How many axes are worth reading, and how faithful the diagram is. #> autoplot(ord, type = "scree")   # or type = "shepard" #> Plots: Biplot with numeric variables as contours or symbol size, factors as #> centroids; scree or Shepard inset; stability ellipses #> Contours show non-linear change that an arrow hides; the inset shows how #> faithful the diagram is; ellipses show which sites are placed firmly. #> autoplot(ord, surface = <numeric>, colour = <factor>, inset = "scree")   # "shepard" for NMDS #> autoplot(ord, type = "gradient", path = <numeric>) #> autoplot(ord, type = "stability") #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the tables and the diagram #> Variation explained, tests, directions of variables, groups, species at each #> end of the axes, and how to read the plot. #> ord_interpret(ord) cases <- data.frame(   week = seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), by = "week", length.out = 12),   n = c(2, 3, 5, 4, 9, 12, 15, 24, 30, 41, 60, 77) ) tidyvisor(cases, question = "epidemic", date = "week", cases = "n") #>  #> ── tidyvisor: how fast is the epidemic growing? ──────────────────────────────── #> Question: epidemic #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Records: 12 #> • Time points: 12 #> • Dispersion about the trend (Pearson): 0.1 — close to Poisson #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Approach: Exponential growth rate from a log-linear count model #> Early in an outbreak cases grow exponentially; the slope of log cases on time #> is the growth rate r. #> Method: Poisson generalised linear model over the exponential phase #> Choose a window where the log counts rise in a straight line; later, control #> and depletion bend the curve. #> g <- epi_growth_rate(data, date = week, cases = n, family = "poisson", window = c(<start>, <end>)) #> Reproduction number: Convert r to R with the generation interval #> R depends on r and on the mean and standard deviation of the generation #> interval (Wallinga and Lipsitch 2007); take these from the literature for the #> pathogen. #> epi_growth_rate(..., generation_mean = <mean>, generation_sd = <sd>) #> Spatial spread: Simulate spread across hosts with a dispersal kernel #> To ask where an infection could go, combine host density, transmission and a #> dispersal kernel. #> geo_epidemic_simulate(hosts, init_inf, beta = <beta>, gamma = <gamma>, dispersal_mean = <km>) #> Plots: Observed counts with the fitted curve and its confidence band, on a log #> scale #> On a log scale exponential growth is a straight line, so departures from it are #> easy to see. #> plot(g) #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the estimates #> tidyvisor(g)

code: tidyvisor(kruskal.test(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays)) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test on count by spray. #>  #> ── Result ── #>  #> • Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 54.7 (df = 5), p < 0.001. #>  #> ── Meaning ── #>  #> • Values in one group tend to be larger than in another. Rank tests compare #>   whole distributions, not means: report medians or the location shift with its #>   interval, not a difference in means. #> • A p-value is not the size of an effect: always report the estimate and its #>   interval, and a non-significant result is not evidence of no difference. #>  #> ── After the overall test ── #>  #> • The overall test shows that the 6 groups are not all alike; it does not say #>   which differ. Go on to post hoc comparisons of every pair, with p-values #>   adjusted for the number of comparisons. #> • Rank-based pairs (the follow-up to Kruskal-Wallis): #>   pairwise.wilcox.test(data$count, data$spray, p.adjust.method = "holm"), or a #>   Dunn test (FSA::dunnTest(count ~ spray, data = data, method = "holm")). #> • Report each pair as a median difference or Hodges-Lehmann shift with its #>   interval (wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE)), not only adjusted p-values. #> • Decide which pairs matter before looking: if only comparisons with a control #>   are of interest, test those alone (Dunnett, or Holm on that smaller set); #>   fewer comparisons keep more power. #>  #> ── What to do next ── #>  #> • For an effect size, wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE) gives the Hodges-Lehmann #>   shift with its interval. #> • If the data are positive and right-skewed, a test on the log scale (or a #>   Gamma GLM) gives a ratio of means, which is often easier to report. #>  #> ── For the paper ── #>  #> • Results: 'count differed among levels of spray (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test; #>   H(5) = 54.7, p < 0.001).' #> • Report the statistic with its degrees of freedom, the exact p-value (p < #>   0.001 below that), and the effect size with its interval; never 'p = 0.000' #>   or 'n.s.' alone. #> • Figure: #> • ggplot2::ggplot(data, ggplot2::aes(spray, count)) + #>   ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) + #>   ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) + #>   ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 9) #> • ggplot2::ggsave("figure1.pdf", width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm") # one #>   journal column #> • Figure style for journals: show the raw data with the estimates, give n per #>   group in the caption, label axes with units, use a colour-blind-safe palette #>   (Okabe-Ito, viridis) and no 3D, pie or dual-axis charts; text at least 8 pt #>   at final size; save as PDF or SVG (vector) at the journal's column width #>   (about 85 mm single, 180 mm double), or 600 dpi for raster images. #> • Table: one row per level of spray with n and the median and interquartile #>   range; the test in a footnote, and any post hoc results as letters or a #>   pairwise table with adjusted p-values. #> • Methods: name the test (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test), the software and #>   version (R 4.3.3, citation()), any adjustment for multiple comparisons, and #>   the significance level. tidyvisor(glm(count ~ spray, family = poisson, data = InsectSprays)) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Generalised linear model of count on 72 observations (poisson family, log #>   link). #>  #> ── Fit ── #>  #> • The predictors explain 76.0% of the deviance (the GLM analogue of R-squared). #> • Against a model with no predictors: likelihood-ratio chi-squared = 310.7 on 5 #>   df, p < 0.001. #>  #> ── Effects ── #>  #> • sprayB: spray = B (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   1.06 (+6%; 95% CI 0.860 to 1.30), p = 0.597. #> • sprayC: spray = C (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   0.144 (-86%; 95% CI 0.0945 to 0.218), p < 0.001. #> • sprayD: spray = D (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   0.339 (-66%; 95% CI 0.252 to 0.456), p < 0.001. #> • sprayE: spray = E (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   0.241 (-76%; 95% CI 0.172 to 0.338), p < 0.001. #> • sprayF: spray = F (compared with spray = A) multiplies the expected count by #>   1.15 (+15%; 95% CI 0.938 to 1.41), p = 0.179. #> • Effects on the log or logit scale are multiplicative: they combine by #>   multiplying, and a factor of 1 means no effect. #> • Each effect is estimated with the other predictors held fixed. #>  #> ── Diagnostics ── #>  #> • Overdispersion: Pearson statistic / residual df = 1.51 (expected about 1). #>   Standard errors and p-values are too small; refit with a negative binomial #>   model (MASS::glm.nb()) or family = quasipoisson. #> • Influence: no observation dominates the fit (largest Cook's distance 0.19, #>   row 27; values above 1 would be a concern). #>  #> ── After the overall test ── #>  #> • spray (6 levels) has an overall effect (p < 0.001): the levels are not all #>   alike. Go on to post hoc comparisons of every pair, adjusted for the number #>   of comparisons; the coefficients above only compare each level with the #>   reference level A. #> • emmeans::emmeans(m, pairwise ~ spray, type = "response") # Tukey-adjusted #>   pairs, with intervals #> • If only comparisons with a control matter, decide so before looking and use #>   emmeans::emmeans(m, trt.vs.ctrl ~ spray, type = "response") (Dunnett; the #>   first level, A, is the control), which keeps more power. #>  #> ── For the paper ── #>  #> • Results (strongest evidence first; each factor level is compared with the #>   reference level): #> • 'count was 0.144 times as high for spray = C as for spray = A (95% CI 0.0945 #>   to 0.218, p < 0.001).' #> • 'count was 0.241 times as high for spray = E as for spray = A (95% CI 0.172 #>   to 0.338, p < 0.001).' #> • 'count was 0.339 times as high for spray = D as for spray = A (95% CI 0.252 #>   to 0.456, p < 0.001).' #> • The model is on the log scale, so effects are reported as ratios of means #>   (exponentiated coefficients) with their intervals. #> • Report every term of the model, not only the significant ones, with the #>   estimate, its 95% CI and the p-value; give n, and the fit (R-squared, or #>   deviance explained, or the random-effect SDs for a mixed model). #> • Figure: model predictions with their confidence band over the raw data, one #>   panel per focal predictor: #> • ggeffects::ggpredict(m, terms = "spray") |> plot(show_data = TRUE) #> • ggplot2::ggsave("figure1.pdf", width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm") # one #>   journal column #> • Figure style for journals: show the raw data with the estimates, give n per #>   group in the caption, label axes with units, use a colour-blind-safe palette #>   (Okabe-Ito, viridis) and no 3D, pie or dual-axis charts; text at least 8 pt #>   at final size; save as PDF or SVG (vector) at the journal's column width #>   (about 85 mm single, 180 mm double), or 600 dpi for raster images. #> • Table: one row per term with the estimate, 95% CI and p-value (and the #>   random-effect SDs for a mixed model): #> • gtsummary::tbl_regression(m, exponentiate = TRUE) # or broom::tidy(m, #>   conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) for your own table #> • Methods: the model formula, the family and link, how the model was checked, #>   the software and packages with versions (R 4.3.3; citation("stats")), and how #>   the predictors were chosen (before seeing the data, or how). #>  #> ── Reading the plots ── #>  #> • plot(model) shows four diagnostics: residuals against fitted values (look for #>   curves or a funnel), the normal Q-Q plot, scale-location (spread against #>   fitted values) and residuals against leverage (influential points). #> • Plot each effect on the response scale, with its confidence band, rather than #>   the coefficients alone.

code: tidyvisor(mtcars, question = "bayesian", response = "am", predictors = "wt") #>  #> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: bayesian #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Observations: 32 #> • Response: binary (two outcomes) #> • Parameters (excluding intercept): 1 #> • Events of the rarer outcome: 13 #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Model: Bayesian regression model with brms (bernoulli()) #> A yes/no response is binomial; the logit link gives effects as odds ratios. #> Weakly informative priors keep estimates in a plausible range without #> dominating the data (Buerkner 2017). #> priors <- c(brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = b)) #> m <- brms::brm(am ~ wt, family = bernoulli(), prior = priors, #>   data = data, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1) #> Before fitting: Prior predictive check #> Simulate from the priors alone to see that they allow plausible data and rule #> out absurd data (Gabry et al. 2019). #> p <- brms::brm(am ~ wt, family = bernoulli(), prior = priors, data = data, sample_prior = "only") #> brms::pp_check(p) #> After fitting: Check convergence, then the posterior predictive fit #> R-hat must be below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400 before any #> estimate is read (Vehtari et al. 2021). #> summary(m); brms::pp_check(m); brms::loo(m) #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the model #> Effects with credible intervals and the probability of their direction. #> tidyvisor(m)

A count GLM models #> that directly and gives each group difference as a ratio of means; transforming #> counts (log(y + 1)) biases the estimates (O'Hara and Kotze 2010). The variance #> is up to 2.3 times the mean, so the negative binomial. #> m <- MASS::glm.nb(count ~ spray, data = data) #> anova(m, test = "Chisq"); tidyvisor(m) #> Alternative: Non-parametric: rank test #> Makes no assumption about the shape of the distributions; answers whether #> values in one group tend to be larger. #> kruskal.test(count ~ spray, data = data) #> pairwise.wilcox.test(data$count, data$spray, p.adjust.method = "holm") #> Alternative: Robust: trimmed means #> Resists outliers and heavy tails while still comparing a centre. #> WRS2::t1way(count ~ spray, data = data)   # 20% trimmed means #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the result #> What was tested, the effect with its interval, and what to do next. #> tidyvisor(result) tidyvisor(kruskal.test(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays)) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test on count by spray. #>  #> ── Result ── #>  #> • Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 54.7 (df = 5), p < 0.001. #>  #> ── Meaning ── #>  #> • Values in one group tend to be larger than in another. Rank tests compare #>   whole distributions, not means: report medians or the location shift with its #>   interval, not a difference in means. #> • A p-value is not the size of an effect: always report the estimate and its #>   interval, and a non-significant result is not evidence of no difference. #>  #> ── After the overall test ── #>  #> • The overall test shows that the 6 groups are not all alike; it does not say #>   which differ. Go on to post hoc comparisons of every pair, with p-values #>   adjusted for the number of comparisons. #> • Rank-based pairs (the follow-up to Kruskal-Wallis): #>   pairwise.wilcox.test(data$count, data$spray, p.adjust.method = "holm"), or a #>   Dunn test (FSA::dunnTest(count ~ spray, data = data, method = "holm")). #> • Report each pair as a median difference or Hodges-Lehmann shift with its #>   interval (wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE)), not only adjusted p-values. #> • Decide which pairs matter before looking: if only comparisons with a control #>   are of interest, test those alone (Dunnett, or Holm on that smaller set); #>   fewer comparisons keep more power. #>  #> ── What to do next ── #>  #> • For an effect size, wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE) gives the Hodges-Lehmann #>   shift with its interval. #> • If the data are positive and right-skewed, a test on the log scale (or a #>   Gamma GLM) gives a ratio of means, which is often easier to report. #>  #> ── For the paper ── #>  #> • Results: 'count differed among levels of spray (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test; #>   H(5) = 54.7, p < 0.001).' #> • Report the statistic with its degrees of freedom, the exact p-value (p < #>   0.001 below that), and the effect size with its interval; never 'p = 0.000' #>   or 'n.s.' alone. #> • Figure: #> • ggplot2::ggplot(data, ggplot2::aes(spray, count)) + #>   ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) + #>   ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) + #>   ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 9) #> • ggplot2::ggsave("figure1.pdf", width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm") # one #>   journal column #> • Figure style for journals: show the raw data with the estimates, give n per #>   group in the caption, label axes with units, use a colour-blind-safe palette #>   (Okabe-Ito, viridis) and no 3D, pie or dual-axis charts; text at least 8 pt #>   at final size; save as PDF or SVG (vector) at the journal's column width #>   (about 85 mm single, 180 mm double), or 600 dpi for raster images. #> • Table: one row per level of spray with n and the median and interquartile #>   range; the test in a footnote, and any post hoc results as letters or a #>   pairwise table with adjusted p-values. #> • Methods: name the test (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test), the software and #>   version (R 4.6.2, citation()), any adjustment for multiple comparisons, and #>   the significance level.

random intercepts for #> Subject account for it and let the results generalise to other groups (Bolker #> et al. 2009). #> m <- lme4::lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = data) #> Random slopes: Consider a random slope for a predictor that varies within #> groups #> If the effect of a predictor differs among groups, a random intercept alone #> makes its p-value too small. #> (1 + Days | Subject) #> Before fitting: Plot the response against each predictor #> Shows non-linear relations, outliers and interactions that the model would miss #> (Zuur et al. 2010). #> plot(data[c("Reaction", "Days")]) #> After fitting: Check the residuals #> Residual plots show non-linearity, unequal variance and influential points; #> tidyvisor reports the tests. #> plot(m)   # or performance::check_model(m) #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the model #> Fixed effects on the scale of the response, random-effect variances and #> diagnostics. #> tidyvisor(m) m <- lme4::lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = lme4::sleepstudy) tidyvisor(m) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • Linear mixed model of Reaction on 180 observations in 18 levels of Subject #>   (gaussian family, identity link), fitted with lme4. #>  #> ── Random effects ── #>  #> • Subject: (Intercept) varies with a standard deviation of 37.1 (in units of #>   Reaction). #> • Residual standard deviation 31.0. For small samples, use lmerTest or a #>   parametric bootstrap. #> • Fixed effects are for a typical group (random effects at zero), with the #>   other predictors held fixed. #>  #> ── Diagnostics ── #>  #> • Normality of residuals (Shapiro-Wilk): W = 0.975, p = 0.003; Refit with log(mpg) and check #>   again; effects then multiply mpg (report exp(coefficient)). MASS::boxcox(m) #>   shows which power suits the data (0 = log, 0.5 = square root). #> • Or keep the original scale with a Gamma GLM and a log link, which expects the #>   spread to grow with the mean: glm(mpg ~ wt + hp, family = Gamma(link = #>   "log"), data = data). #> • Rank-based or permutation alternatives make no assumption about the #>   distribution: for one factor, kruskal.test() or wilcox.test();
